cards.attribution: Keyes Axiom No. 15 — added 2026-08-13

cards.quote: What we do in life echoes in eternity.
cards.author: Maximus Decimus Meridius
cards.attribution: Gladiator (2000) — written by David Franzoni, John Logan & William Nicholson
cards.back: Maximus says this to steady his cavalry before the opening battle in Germania — a fictional general in a film about a real Stoic court. The irony is worth keeping: Marcus Aurelius, the emperor Maximus serves, spends much of the actual Meditations reminding himself that posthumous fame is worthless, that even the longest-remembered names dissolve. So why does the movie line still land? Because it isn't about fame. It's about consequence. Actions propagate through the people they touch, and those people act on others, far past your sight and your lifetime. You don't get to be remembered; you do get to be causal. Read that way, the Hollywood line and the Stoic emperor stop arguing with each other.

cards.quote: Be the change you want to see in the world.
cards.author: Attributed to Mahatma Gandhi
cards.attribution: Apocryphal condensation — closest verified source is Gandhi's 1913 writings
cards.back: Gandhi almost certainly never said it in these words. The closest verified passage, from 1913, runs: "If we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change... We need not wait to see what others do." The bumper-sticker version compresses his point without betraying it: the only reform you fully control is your own conduct, and personal reform is not a substitute for changing the world — it is the mechanism. It pairs naturally with the golden rule: both refuse to let your behavior wait on anyone else's. The attribution caveat is worth carrying on the card; being honest about sources is itself part of the change.

cards.quote: Treat others as you would want to be treated.
cards.author: Jesus of Nazareth
cards.attribution: Matthew 7:12 / Luke 6:31 — the Sermon on the Mount
cards.back: Nearly every tradition has a version of this rule, but most state it negatively — Hillel: "What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow"; Confucius: "Do not impose on others what you do not desire." The Sermon on the Mount formulation is distinctive because it is positive and therefore active: not merely refrain from harm, but go find the good you'd want done and do it first. That flips the rule from a restraint into an assignment. It also quietly assumes the work of the Self-Command cards — you have to actually know how you'd want to be treated, honestly, before you can extend it outward.

cards.quote: The windshield in front of you is much larger than the rear-view mirror for a reason.
cards.author: Folk wisdom
cards.attribution: Unattributed — common in coaching and motivational circles; origin unknown
cards.back: Nobody owns this one; it circulates through coaching rooms, locker rooms, and sales floors, and its power is in the proportions. The mirror isn't removed — a driver who never checks it is dangerous — it's just sized to the job: quick, deliberate glances backward in service of moving forward. The design of the car is a prescription for attention. Reflection has a place; rumination does not get the whole windshield. Where the Keyes axiom on cognizance asks "do you know where you are?", this one asks "which direction is your glass facing?" — and reminds you the ratio was decided by people who wanted you to survive the trip.

cards.quote: Before pointing out the splinter in another's eye, remove the plank from your own.
cards.author: Jesus of Nazareth
cards.attribution: Matthew 7:3–5 — the Sermon on the Mount
cards.back: The image is deliberately absurd — a man with a beam of lumber through his own eye performing eye surgery on his neighbor — and the absurdity is the argument. Judgment isn't forbidden here; it's sequenced. The passage ends "then you will see clearly to remove the speck," which means the goal is still clear sight and even correction — but self-audit is the prerequisite, not an optional virtue. The plank also explains why hypocrisy is uniquely blinding: your own faults don't just discredit your critique, they distort the very perception the critique depends on. Order of operations: instrument check before measurement.

cards.quote: You shall know them by the fruits of their labor.
cards.author: Jesus of Nazareth
cards.attribution: After Matthew 7:16–20 — "by their fruits ye shall know them"
cards.back: The original context is a warning about false prophets — people whose words are precisely engineered to pass inspection. So the test moves to something harder to fake: output over time. A tree cannot sustain fruit contrary to its nature; a person cannot sustain results contrary to their character. Note the patience built into the metaphor — fruit takes a season, so the verdict isn't available on day one, and one bad apple isn't the harvest. As an evaluation tool it's the ancestor of every "show me, don't tell me": trust trajectories and track records, discount manifestos. And it points back at yourself first — your own fruit is also on display.

cards.quote: Walk softly and carry a big stick.
cards.author: Theodore Roosevelt
cards.attribution: TR's version: "Speak softly and carry a big stick" — 1901, citing a West African proverb
cards.back: Roosevelt introduced it at the Minnesota State Fair in 1901, crediting a West African proverb: "Speak softly and carry a big stick; you will go far." As foreign policy it meant negotiating quietly while the fleet made the quiet credible. The personal version is the same mechanic: courtesy backed by capability. The soft walk without the stick is timidity that invites the test; the stick without the soft walk is a bully looking for one. The proverb only works with both halves installed — and the stick's whole purpose is to be visible enough that it never has to move. Peterson's sheathed sword is this idea wearing different clothes.

cards.quote: Actions speak louder than words.
cards.author: English proverb
cards.attribution: Traced to 17th-century England — a 1628 speech associated with John Pym; Gersham Bulkeley's Will and Doom (1692) has "actions are more significant than words"
cards.back: The sentiment is ancient, but the English paper trail runs through the 1600s: a parliamentary speech from the era of John Pym — "a word spoken in season is like an apple of gold... but a good deed is better" in spirit — and Gersham Bulkeley's 1692 tract Will and Doom, which states it nearly in the modern form. It survived four centuries because it's an information-theory claim, not a moral one: words are cheap to produce, so they carry little signal; action is costly, so it carries a lot. Talk is a bid; behavior is the payment. Its cousin on this deck is the fruits card — same test, agricultural metaphor.

cards.quote: Keep your sword sheathed, but know how to use it.
cards.author: Jordan Peterson
cards.attribution: Peterson's gloss on Matthew 5:5 — "blessed are the meek" read as controlled strength
cards.back: Peterson's rendering of the Beatitude turns on the Greek praus — the word translated "meek," which was also used for war-horses: immense power, trained to command. His paraphrase — those who have swords and know how to use them, but keep them sheathed, will inherit the world — is a contested translation but a very old ethic: harmlessness is only a virtue when harm was an option. A person with no capacity for force isn't peaceful, just safe. The sheathed sword requires two disciplines at once: the years of training that make the blade real, and the daily restraint that keeps it put away. Roosevelt's big stick is the statecraft edition.

cards.quote: The wrong action now is better than the perfect action later.
cards.author: After Gen. George S. Patton
cards.attribution: Patton, War As I Knew It: "A good plan violently executed now is better than a perfect plan executed next week"
cards.back: Patton's actual line, from War As I Knew It, is "a good plan violently executed now is better than a perfect plan executed next week." The Keyes compression pushes it further — even the wrong action beats the perfect one that never ships — and that's defensible on Patton's own logic: in a moving situation, waiting is not neutral. The perfect plan is being drafted against a battlefield that no longer exists, while action generates the one thing planning can't: contact with reality, and information. The caveat lives in the deck's discipline column — this is a doctrine for reversible decisions and fluid situations, not for the handful of one-way doors.

cards.quote: Who you surround yourself with reflects who you are and who you can become.
cards.author: After Jim Rohn
cards.attribution: Rohn: "You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with"
cards.back: Rohn's "average of five" is a motivational heuristic, not a measurement — but the direction of the claim has real support. The Framingham network studies found that obesity, smoking, and even happiness propagate through social ties, out to friends-of-friends. Norms are contagious; your circle quietly sets your baseline for what's normal effort, normal honesty, normal ambition. The Keyes rewording adds two things Rohn's version lacks: the mirror (your current circle is diagnostic — you chose it) and the trajectory (it bounds who you can become, not just who you are). The actionable edge pairs with the investment axiom: curate deliberately, and invest where investment is met.

cards.quote: Know thyself.
cards.author: Delphic maxim, via Socrates
cards.attribution: Inscribed at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi; made a method by Socrates (Plato's Apology)
cards.back: The words predate Socrates — γνῶθι σεαυτόν was carved at the entrance to Apollo's temple at Delphi, a warning to pilgrims about to ask a god for answers: audit the asker first. Socrates turned the inscription into a life's method, examining himself and everyone else in Athens until they killed him for it, insisting that the unexamined life is not worth living. Two thousand years on it remains step zero of this whole deck: the internal-state axiom assumes you can read your own gauges; the plank assumes you'll look for it; the middle path assumes you know which extreme is currently seducing you. Every other card is downstream of this one.

cards.quote: If you are comfortable with yourself, others will be comfortable with you.
cards.author: Folk wisdom
cards.attribution: Unattributed — common counsel; phrasing as collected by JBK
cards.back: Unattributed, and probably unattributable — this is the kind of line that gets re-derived in every generation because people keep observing the same mechanic: emotional states are contagious, and anxiety about the self is among the most contagious of all. A person at ease signals that nothing here needs managing, and the room relaxes to match. The inverse explains most social friction — discomfort with yourself outsources the discomfort to everyone around you, who can feel the performance without being able to name it. Note what the line doesn't promise: not that everyone will like you, only that they'll be at ease. Downstream of know thyself; you can't be comfortable with a stranger.

cards.quote: Strive for the middle path.
cards.author: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha
cards.attribution: After the first sermon (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta) — the Middle Way
cards.back: The Buddha's authority on this one is biographical: he had run both experiments personally — a prince's palace of indulgence, then years of asceticism severe enough to nearly kill him — and found that both extremes make the same error of letting an extreme do your thinking. The Middle Way of his first sermon is not moderation-as-mediocrity or splitting every difference; it's the recognition that extremes are usually easier than judgment. Total indulgence and total denial both remove the daily decision. The middle path is harder precisely because it must be found again each day, by an awake person. The internal-state axiom's 20–80 band is the same instinct with percentages on it.

cards.quote: Before I do anything I ask myself, 'Would an idiot do that?' And if the answer is yes, I do not do that thing.
cards.author: Dwight Schrute
cards.attribution: The Office (US), "Business School" (2007) — written by Brent Forrester, performed by Rainn Wilson
cards.back: A joke that survives contact with philosophy. Dwight's filter is a genuine via negativa — the decision procedure Charlie Munger spent a career preaching as inversion: don't ask what a wise move looks like, ask what a stupid one looks like and don't do that. It works because failure modes are far more predictable than success modes; there are a thousand ways to be clever and about six ways to be an idiot, and the six are well documented. The comedy is that Dwight applies it with total sincerity, which is also the instruction. It earns its place in a wisdom deck the honest way: it's cheap, it's fast, and it catches real errors before they ship.

cards.quote: If you can have fun, you've got it figured out.
cards.author: Joe Rogan
cards.attribution: Recurring sentiment across The Joe Rogan Experience
cards.back: A recurring Rogan refrain rather than a single citable moment, and easy to misread as "optimize for pleasure." The stronger reading is diagnostic: fun is a trailing indicator of a life in working order. Genuine fun — not numbing, not escape — requires present attention, low background dread, people you actually like, and enough command of your obligations that they aren't screaming. If you can still laugh in the middle of hard work, the systems are healthy; if nothing is fun anymore, something upstream is broken, and no achievement will patch it. That makes fun worth monitoring the way you'd monitor sleep. It's the deck's least solemn card and possibly its most honest gauge.

cards.quote: Strength and honor.
cards.author: Gladiator (2000)
cards.attribution: Maximus and his officers' salute — written by Franzoni, Logan & Nicholson, in the style of a Roman military greeting
cards.back: In the film it's how Maximus and his officers greet and part — two words traded like a handshake before battle. It compresses an entire ethic into a breath: strength, the capability to act; honor, the constraint on how. Either word alone is a warning sign — strength without honor is a warlord, honor without strength is a bystander with good intentions. As a battle cry it works because it's a checklist you can say in one exhale: am I bringing both today? Its natural pair in this deck is the Keyes axiom on what's eternal; love, truth, and honor is the longer creed this salute abbreviates for field use.

cards.quote: Today is a good day today.
cards.author: Joshua B. Keyes
cards.attribution: JBK phrasing — echoes the Lakota war cry "Today is a good day to die," recorded from Low Dog (1881)

cards.quote: They've surrounded us? Good — at least we know where they are.
cards.author: After Lt. Gen. Lewis "Chesty" Puller, USMC
cards.attribution: Chosin Reservoir, Korea, 1950 — "We've finally found the enemy. We're surrounded. That simplifies our problem."
cards.back: At the Chosin Reservoir in 1950, the 1st Marine Division was encircled by vastly larger Chinese forces in minus-thirty-degree cold. Puller's remark — variations survive, all in the same key: "We're surrounded. That simplifies our problem" — wasn't denial. The Marines fought their way out with their wounded, their equipment, and the division intact. The reframe is the weapon: the facts of the situation are fixed, but the framing decides what the situation is for. Uncertainty is heavier than bad news; at least the located enemy can be engaged. As a daily card, it's for the moment the problems all arrive at once — good, no more guessing where they are.

cards.quote: Never give up, never surrender!
cards.author: Cmdr. Peter Quincy Taggart
cards.attribution: Galaxy Quest (1999) — a parody catchphrase that earned its sincerity; echoes Churchill at Harrow, 1941: "Never give in"
cards.back: The joke of Galaxy Quest is that a washed-up actor's hollow catchphrase gets taken literally by aliens who built a civilization on reruns — and the arc of the film is the phrase becoming true, because people kept acting as if it were. That's a real mechanic wearing a comedy costume: creeds work by repetition before belief. Its serious ancestor is Churchill at Harrow in 1941 — "never give in, never, never, never... except to convictions of honour and good sense" — and Churchill's forgotten exception matters: persistence is for worthy aims, not sunk costs. Keep the exception in the footnote and the war cry in your mouth.
